sources.entry: After Being A Manager, Can I Be Happy As A Cog?

summary.title: Questionable Advice: "After Being A Manager, Can I Be Happy As A Cog?"
summary.one_liner: A reader who left a two-year management role asks whether they can go back to being an individual contributor, and Charity Majors argues that senior ICs should reclaim technical decision-making rather than see IC work as a demotion.
keywords: service teams own code in production
takeaways: Going back to an IC role after management often feels like a loss of power and status, and that feeling is real in most hierarchical orgs.
Senior ICs who have managed carry influence and can act as mentors or shadow managers for good managers.
Reaching the two-to-three-year mark in management makes returning to hands-on technical work harder over time.
Technical decisions should generally sit with technical people and people decisions with managers; senior ICs must claim that ownership for it to happen.
Organizations are shaped by the people in them, so senior ICs can push for structures where management is a career change, not a promotion.
summary.summary: This is an advice column post from Charity Majors' blog, part of a series she started in 2019 answering reader questions. It reprints an anonymized letter from a former manager who led a successful shift to devops and cloud, but found the day-to-day of management draining and feared becoming a small cog as an IC. The response is opinionated and conversational, arguing the company likely undervalues the reader, that management usually carries more power, and that senior ICs should push to own technical decisions. The piece ends with encouragement to find a healthier company and to share experiences through writing and talks.
